She invites her to stay in Genoa. Various instructions about the Genoa Sisters and the Superior at Sampierdarena. She should ask the Superiors to supply her with pharmacy goods.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I have just received yours and hear you say you will come on Tuesday.1 Listen, God alone knows how glad I would be to see you, but on the other hand I am pleased that you are staying to take the baths, so you will grow ever stronger.

  2. Listen, don't bring me sisters either to be unfrocked or to be clothed;2 let them be unfrocked there, which will set a better example. You can tell Sr. A. Giusta that I give her eight days to mend her ways; if she does not, she will be sent away.3 You see, if an example is made on the spot, they will be more afraid and do better. For the rest, let us hope.

  1. Only urge the Superior4 never to miss the exercises of piety and the common acts. If she is always punctual at these, she will see her community become a true mirror and all will go well. So she must never miss them, for pity's sake.

  2. Gaspare must be careful of the sun, it is terrible; I commend the Little Doll to you, don't let them keep her in the sun. Oh! I am frightened for the children! Take care.

  3. Tell Sr. A. Amabile that she and the others should supply me with a few chemist's goods, namely: a large bottle of castor oil, another big one of magnesia, another of cream of tartar and another of milk sugar, galerina and mustard papers,5 and some whole linseed. Oh! It would be a real godsend, for then I would not have so many bills.

6. My God! When I think of those for the Morte, which come to more than two thousand F.,6 and then all the rest, it really makes me suffer! Enough. God will see to it. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 In the L of 19 July she told her she would return on Tuesday (23 July).

2 She had written to her about some Sisters who were not behaving well, saying she would bring them to Piacenza to send them back to their families.

3 Sr. A. Giusta asked the Mother's forgiveness.

4 To the Superior: Sr. A. Claudia Tabarrini, whom Sr. A. Benedetta had accompanied to Sampierdarena.

5 Galerina: a medicine. Mustard papers.

6 Those for the Morte: the bills and expenses of the house in Via della Morte, the infirmary for the Sisters.

Spiritual advice on humility and on one's attitude towards Superiors.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you that if you want to be a true daughter of Saint Anne and become a saint, there is one thing only you must seek to have, and that is humility; if you have it, you will obtain the love of God and become a saint.^2 ^Without this treasure of humility you can have no good.

2. We must see our Superiors in the place of God, and so we must love and fear them.3 There is no true love without fear: fear, if you would love!

Sure of obtaining from my daughter what I tell her, I wish you a thousand blessings, and remain your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The date is deduced from the context.

2 The "true" FSA strives to place herself before God in an attitude of humility, looking to Christ who lowered himself to the utmost humiliation.

3 Our Superiors... love! Humility and faith in relations with Superiors too. To see them in the place of God and love them in the "holy fear of God". One is asked to "do the truth" and live in its light.

She answers her letter with a word of encouragement.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear so much good news from the Superior1 and I also see your joy at the thought of having a fine house.2

  2. Ah! Blessed be God who does all things well and thinks of us besides, wretched creatures that we are. So be cheerful, for we shall see each other soon. Your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior, Illuminata Cavassa, had come to the Mother House for the Exercises and had reported on the House in Vicolo Margana, Rome, and on the new work.

2 Your joy at having a fine house. This refers to the beginning of a new work already under negotiation: the "Casa delle Ravvedute" in Via dei Riari on the Lungara.

She has received the letters but awaits more news of the new house. They should ask the administrators to accept another Sister. Advice on observance and encouragement.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received your letters and hear that it is hard for you to keep the observance. 1 For pity's sake, ask these good administrators to grant you one more sister, as I am now writing to the Co.2

  2. For the rest, I cannot wait for you to tell me what salary they pay you, and also see that you do not open outside schools unless they have first called two more Sisters. Do you understand?

  3. Tell my Sr. A. Sempliciana so, and tell her too that I am not answering her because I am weighed down with work, but I hope towards the end of this month to write her a whole exercise book.3 Meanwhile you must always write to me and not leave me without your letters. Courage, and stand firm by the Rules. A thousand deaths, but observant; and if you do so, be assured that you will be with me in Heaven for all eternity.4

God bless you; ever your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The three Sisters requested to direct and run the orphanage had arrived at Termini Imerese on 17 July, but finding great disorder they had not yet managed, with so much work, to fix a complete timetable.

1 I

Termini Imerese. Embroidery workshop.

2 An extra Sister was indispensable, not least because of the large number of orphans, 54 in all, some of them older. She will write to the Commission.

3 Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti was the teaching Sister. At the end of the month she will write her a whole exercise book, the Mother jokes.

4 With me in Heaven. The goal to strive for was to be uppermost in their thoughts, as the one purpose of the present life.

She reassures her. She is delighted with her work. She does not write because she is extremely busy.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Oh! my dear daughter, not only am I convinced that you are all mine and that I am the only one, but rest assured, I am delighted.1 Listen, for your information: oh! if I could I would fly to you! Listen, the weight of work is such that at times it does not let me either sleep or...2 Oh! blessed toil!!3 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

In a few days you will have the Sister; yours for all ages,

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Mother's silence made her fearful, attributing it to some unwitting fault of her own.

2 She leaves the thought unfinished.

3 Toil is blessed because it is necessary for God's Work.

Unable to reply because of too much work. Advice on how to behave with outsiders.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear so many good things, but you would like me to answer at once, and that is impossible.1 If you could see how much I have to do! I must have taken up this letter more than 20 times!2

  2. Listen, be patient and try to do everything in order. Always be accompanied, never, never alone.3

  3. Yes, you must be the Institute's showpiece,4 and if you do well and bear fine fruit everyone will want a branch of your tree; so courage, and goodbye. Your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior had sent her reports on the new work and wanted specific directions on everything. Cf. Index IV, Termini Imerese.

2 She had much to do. The Superiors had arrived in Piacenza and she had to hear them. The Exercises for all began on 5 August. She had to take decisions and deal with correspondence, not only with her Daughters.

3 She meant: never deal alone with outsiders, such as the administrators.

4 The showpiece: to be the exemplary image of the Institute.

She rebukes her, urging her to be prudent in speech and behaviour towards the Sisters and Fr Accinelli.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Listen, I really wish you were a little more prudent in speech, for instance not saying to the sisters: "You are here for your bread." You see that is not right.1 So I hope you have come back to yourself2 and will try to speak a little more quietly, otherwise everyone hears you.3

  2. Fr Accinelli is offended, because he says the sisters (who did wrong to tell us) say he must not interfere4 (what wicked tongues!). Enough: see that you treat him well as he deserves, and give him my warm regards. I hope it will come to nothing.5 Goodbye, yours. Write to me and be cheerful, for everything will be sorted out; I am your

affectionate M. Rosa

3. Send Sr. A. Gherarda's linen at once, for I don't want any trouble, her mother having threatened me.6

1 The Superior's remark was gravely offensive. But the Mother, knowing her character, measures her words of rebuke carefully: You see that is not right.

2 ... you will have become yourself again, aware of your responsibilities.

3 Everyone hears you. The Sisters' residence was not detached.

4 Accinelli... interfere. He helped the community from outside, promoting its good running with no other aim than esteem and love for the Institute and friend-ship for M. Rosa and the Gattorno family. Certainly he was not to interfere in the community's affairs.

5 She hopes there will be no harmful consequences, that is, Accinelli withdrawing and refusing to concern himself any further with the Daughters of Saint Anne.

6 Sr. A. Gherarda Pastorelli, the novice sent home for lack of vocation.

In the name of Jesus she wishes them "peace", earnestly desiring that peace return, bind them in unity and revive charity. Let murmuring, the devil's work, be trampled underfoot, let them change their lives and let their hearts be set on fire with Love. She awaits a letter promising a sincere change of heart.

A.M.F.

My daughters,

  1. I would like to say a few words that, in the name of the Lord, might be engraved on your hearts;2 and I know nowhere better to find them than in the Most Sacred Heart of that love, Jesus. Daughters! Have pity and listen to me: it is a Mother speaking to you; these are words of that most sweet Heart which, through this wretched and unworthy Mother of yours, comes to make you hear them.

  2. His first word, as the fount of love, urges you to listen to him; he calls you by the name of peace, which shows his earnest desire that peace return to you and that you all love one another in one way,3 held together in one person, your Superior.4

  3. Peace be with you, and may the Spirit of charity be revived in you; may the wicked thing, or rather the monster, of murmuring be trampled underfoot. Oh!!! whispering!

  4. Diabolical spirit, I curse you and command you to leave what does not belong to you, my dearest Community; these are my daughters; the Blood of a God has snatched them from the claws of a corrupt world and set them to fight under his standard; abhorred by the Daughters of Zion, flee, for I curse you.5

  5. My daughters, alas! This name draws tears from me when I think that the seed of tares is among you. You, blessed of the Lord, who well know that you harbour it, tear it out6 of your heart

and bring to the Lord's feet the triumph of victory, your heart free of so foul a monster.

6. Ah, promise me to change your lives; return from the mire to purity, and let your thought be one with mine: to be consumed for Jesus. Be a comfort to me in these moments of toil and sacrifice7 with a letter assuring me that you will put into practice what I tell you, while I hold you all in the most sweet Heart of my Jesus and tell you that I am torn with grief thinking of you. Have pity on me and tell me that you will reform your hearts, so that when I come I may find you as I desire, all Love, where I hope to see you consumed in Jesus; your most sorrowful Mother

Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

1 The date is deduced from some contextual data: the address, Via Stella 120, Palazzo Sannicandro, Naples, where the community was based until 12 October 1878; Sr. A. Speranza Volpini's correspondence with M. Rosa, especially the L of 3 August '78; and other information drawn from events of that period.

2 The Mother aims to enlighten, move and heal the heart.

3 It is a Mother speaking to you, and she speaks the most sweet words of the Heart of Jesus, the first of which is peace. Peace be with you is his gift of love (Jn 20:19). It is the return of unity in one heart (Acts 4:32).

4 Your Superior. She does not name her, but the Mother had decided on a change: the new Superior would be Sr. A. Speranza Volpini, replacing Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti, already assigned to open a new work at S. Maria Capua Vetere but temporarily in Piacenza for the spiritual Exercises.

5 Diabolical spirit... I curse you! The Mother, seized by a surge of indignation and suffering, exorcizes the diabolical Spirit, carrying out Jesus' command: "... cast out demons". Cf. Mt 10:8.

6 Tear it out, pull it up.7Cf. L 113, n. 2.

7 Cf. L 113, n. 2.

She should postpone accepting the postulant. She encloses the teaching Sister's diploma.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A hasty line in answer to yours, just received. 1 I tell you that if the Postulant does not have all, all the money, do not receive her; when she has it all, then accept her; otherwise no, no, no. Your

affectionate M. Rosa This is the diploma.2

1 Sr. A. Santina's L has not been preserved; her reply of 6.8.1878, however, survives.

2 It is Sr. A. Clemenza Marra's diploma. Cf. L 140, n. 5.

She has written to the Mayor, sorry about what is happening in the school. She should send the money for now. After the examinations she expects her in Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I hear you are being harassed; I have written firmly to the Mayor, and that you are to hold the examinations on the 15th of this month;1 and I am very sorry the superior did not come.2 That means that once the examinations are over you can come by yourself and spend a month with me on holiday. Tell the Superior to stay.

  2. If you can, send me 470 F. in two insured letters;3 I expect them at once, and then I expect (you), so that you will have a month of pure holiday with the others.

  3. Goodbye, greet everyone. For this year Sr. A. Fabia must be patient; you will see that another year she will come, having studied a little, and will do better.4 I have no time to write more. Your

affectionate M. Rosa Gattorno

1 On 30 July the Sister had written with bad news: a Royal Commissioner had been appointed, who often visited the school and found pretexts to criticize the nuns' teaching; he wanted lay teachers instead of the Sisters. Among other things he had moved the date of the examinations to 30 September.

2 The Superior was supposed to go to Piacenza for the spiritual exercises. Cf. L 100.

3 Sr. A. Irene already had that sum ready to hand over in person.

4 Sr. A. Fabia De Giorgi had to take the resit examinations, having been referred to the second session.

From Genoa she arranges to meet her in Piacenza and advises her to persuade Canon Biagini to come to Piacenza to settle his testamentary decisions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. I have received yours and see that mine reached you late; I hope you sent Sr. A. Eugenia to Florence at once.1 Now I answer what you tell me, hoping this reaches you in time.

  2. So listen, I shall not be back in Piacenza until Saturday, so it is better for you to leave Pistoia on Monday,2 provided the Canon is agreeable.

  3. How good it would be if we could persuade him to come to Piacenza! He would settle everything with our Bishop. Try to persuade him to come, for it would really be good.3

Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Eugenia Gaudenzi.

2 Monday 12 August.

3 Canon Angelo Biagini. Cf. L 9, n. 4; 27,2-3; 29,1.

Advice for the house and the community.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. A hasty line to tell you that you must tell the Comm.1 at once to buy you everything you need for the beds and linen. For pity's sake, don't catch cold, do you understand?

  2. I would like to say so many things to you and to dear Sr. A. Sempli-ciana;2 everything you wrote to me is fine. I am pleased; the sister 3 has already left and I hope she will be with you. Your

affectionate M. Rosa On Saturday I shall be in Piacenza. 4

1 The Comm., the administrative Commission.

2 Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti.

3 Cf. L 111,1.

4 Saturday 10 August.

She announces a Sister's arrival. She urges silence and prudence. She thanks her for what she has sent.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You will receive this from Sr. A. Teresa.1 Listen, she is a good nurse and so I am sending her back to you; I don't know what else to do, I have no others, so we must be content. Please say nothing to her about the box you mentioned to me.

  2. Silence. Listen, see that no one ever hears you speak of Fr Acc., because unfortunately [...]2 enough; I hope he will come here and so put an end to certain chatter that is truly false and pointless.3

  3. So I have only Sr. A. Elisa; the others are all committed already. If you want her [...]4 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

4. Thank you for the pasta and everything; may the Lord reward you; I hold you in the Heart of Jesus and am your

affectionate M. Rosa

Always send Sr. A. Matilde with someone long in her vocation.5

Sr. A. Teresa Guaini was a good nurse but had poor eyesight. She leaves the sentence unfinished. Cf. L 114,2 and related notes.

3 There was no good understanding between the Superior Amabile and Fr Accinelli. He had complained to the Mother about the conduct of the Superior, "young and light-headed". Cf. L 10.7.1878 to M. Rosa.

4 If you want her I will send her.

5 Sr. A. Matilde Arnedos, a Novice. For prudence, when nursing the sick she should go with an experienced Sister firm in her vocation.

She reassures her and grants the permissions asked for.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. In haste, and besides I am really not well. Listen, set your mind at rest about yourself. Love the sisters and make yourself feared;1 so buy the aprons, and go on the country outing2 as you say; the teacher will be with you soon. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

Present these certificates to the Mayor.3

1 Love and make yourself feared. Love is not weak indulgence at the expense of good order and observance of the Rule.

2 The country outing, a trip to the countryside.

3 The teaching Sisters' qualifications.

She sends her two Sisters to nurse the sick and forbids her to go herself. Advice about alms collecting.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I am sending you two sisters who will help you with the sick.1 First of all I command you under obedience not to go and sit up at night with the sick. Do you understand? I absolutely forbid it; remember you have the vow.2 For the rest, you will see I am sending you Sr. A. Florinda; Sr. A. Santina wants her; do as you think best; if you want to send her there, send her when the sick are done with.3

  2. Tell me, tell me, when can you return that passbook to me, for I need it?4

3. You are right about the collecting; write to the superior in my name and tell her where she is to send them and not to go further.^5^Your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The number of the sick had grown, so help was needed.

2 She commands it, reminding her of the commitment of the vow of obedience.

3 Sr. A. Florinda Viale was a good nurse. The Superior Santina Solenghi had asked for her for Florence. She could send her when the epidemic in Pistoia was over.

4 the house's savings passbook.

5 About the collecting... further. The Florence Sisters had gone collecting from some benefactors of the Pistoia house. It was best to come to an agreement with the Superior Santina so that this would not happen.

She urges her to obtain an artificial eye for a Sister.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. In haste: tell Sr. A. Cirilla at once to give you the damaged eye,1 and send it immediately to the superior in Parma, so that she sends you another at once on my orders.2 I am very glad to hear that she is so happy there; God be blessed. The Lord bless you,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Cirilla Costa wore an artificial eye (a glass eye).

2 The urgency is clearly explained by the pressing need.

She asks her to find out in her name which Sisters are willing to go to America, to note their particulars and then come to her for further instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours and hear that you are upset because I sent Sr. A. Teresa back to you.1 Listen, I shall tell you the reason in person.

2. Listen, do me the kindness of gathering the sisters and saying to them all: "Mother asks which of you wishes to go to America", and having heard them all, note carefully those who want to go and come and tell me yourself, and then I shall tell you in person what to do.2

3. I expect you as soon as possible; we always have half-price tickets;3 go to the stationmaster and have a word with him, and he will speak to the ticket clerk and that will be the end of the whole scene.4 Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 120,1.

2 What to do, prepare documents, photographs, etc.

3 The 50% railway reduction.

4 There will be no need to make requests of other people and be refused.

She encloses a money order to be cashed. She asks for news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line. I hear Alessandro is unwell, but if you don't know where he is, what can be done?1 We must be patient. I enclose a money order; have that Sr. A. Cassandrina sign it above my signature and send it back to me.2 Have you seen Cenni again?3 What does the Archbishop say, is he coming? What are they saying?4 Goodbye, your

Affectionate M. Rosa

1 Cf. L 104, n. 3.

2 Sr. A. Cassandrina Gastaldi, the payee of the order, had to sign it authorizing the Mother to cash it.

3 Sr. A. Costanza Cenni had been at Terricciola in July and beyond, collecting alms.

4 The Archbishop of Florence, Mgr Eugenio Cecconi, had been invited to visit the house. What are they saying? She refers to the familiar problem of the house and wants to know what the priests are saying about it. Cf. L 104, n. 2 and 4.

She need not tire herself studying. She is pleased with all they have organized. She will soon send another Sister.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. I received your registered letter and all is well. Thank you now for the good news you give me; leave the sacristy to Sr. A. Sempliciana, and don't tire yourself studying; I do not allow you to stay up at night;1 you need not study for the diploma; what you know is enough to govern a house well, together with holy observance, which is everything; so sleep.2

  2. As for the door, you did well; when the Sister comes she can take it over; I shall try to make sure she is long in her vocation;3 for now leave the girl there. I tell you, you did well.

3. I am pleased about the little cards too.4 Courage and strength, all for Jesus. I hope Sr. A. Sempliciana has received my other registered letter with the certificate.5

4. The sister I shall send I will have left with the Bishop of Palermo, who will then send her to you, that's right.6 I shall write to him now and hope he will have no objection, because the sisters are to go by way of Catania, and it certainly does not seem to me that there is a passage to your island, since you tell me it is an island;7 so how can it be done? Write to me about it. Goodbye; may the Lord consume you in his divine Love, and one day in the blessed homeland

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The Superior had said she was willing to sacrifice sleep to prepare for the teaching diploma.

2 The Mother reminds her of the concrete reality of her physical and mental limits (proper rest is indispensable after each day of intense, demanding work) and of what is actually needed to carry out the office of Superior.

3 It was good always to have someone at the door. She will assign her a Sister of proven experience.

4 Perhaps they had been prepared for the school.

5 The certificate: the qualification.

6 The Sister would have travelled with those going to Catania on the Naples-Palermo-Catania steamer. She would therefore have landed at Palermo and gone to the Bishop.

7 The Sisters had not expressed themselves clearly. The island they meant was Sicily. Termini Imerese is not on another island.

She announces the arrival of three Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Well done for all you have done; listen, three may be arriving soon,1 and as soon as you have them write to me at once and tell me whether you want one for yourself or can do without; I shall tell you at once where to send them. Courage and keep working; those for America leave soon.2 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. Rosa

1 Three Sisters will arrive at Foligno.

2 Preparations for this were under way. Cf. L 124,2.

She arranges the organization of the Uppello community, asks her to accompany the new Superior to Gualdo Tadino and tells her about the new Superior of Spello.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. You will receive this from the hands of Sr. A. Remigia, whom you will take to the Duchess.1 She is coming as Superior of Uppello; she is a teacher with her diploma in order, and as soon as I can detach it I shall send it at once, so that you can present it; the Duchess will present it.2

  2. Likewise Sr. A. Pierina as her assistant, and (likewise) you will give her another, even a somewhat lame one, for the kitchen; anyone will do, but be sure not to give her Sr. A. Elvira; not her, no.3

  3. Kindly accompany Sr. A. Dorotea to Gualdo Tadino, where she is going to replace Sr. A. Tomasina, and read the enclosed letter to the Sisters.4

  4. Listen, I have told Sr. A. Remigia that she must help you in everything, and I hope she will.

  5. To Spello Sr. A. Carmelita, and I have sent her; I hope she will do well. You will withdraw yours; not for the moment, because she will show her what to do, and then when she has seen, you can certainly take her back.5

  6. Be of good heart, cheerful and content; we do everything for Jesus. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Sr. A. Remigia Montanari. She was to present her to Duchess Agnese Borghese, wife of Prince Boncompagni of Sora Piombino.

2 The qualification to be presented to the school authorities; indeed the Duchess would do so as founder and manager of the Uppello school.

3 The members of the small community: Sr. A. Pierina as assistant in the school, Sr. A. Margherita. Somewhat lame, not in perfect shape.

4 Sr. A. Dorotea Bene goes to Gualdo Tadino to replace Sr. A. Tomasina Viterbo. The enclosed letter has not been preserved.

5 To Spello... take her back. She has already sent Sr. A. Carmelita Rolliamone to Spello. The Sister from Foligno will stay with her until she has trained her.

She was greatly grieved that the Superior did not come to Piacenza for the Exercises. She speaks of the value of obedience and stresses its importance with the example of a Servant of the Lord who "obstinately refused to obey any longer".

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Oh! what grief I felt on hearing that the one who should have set a good example gave scandal by refusing to obey!1 Daughter, the first holiness lies in obeying; I can never believe a soul good that disobeys, still less when it is a matter of submitting a judgement and command of the Superiors to others! Oh! no! no!2

  2. True perfection, turn it, turn it whichever way we like: obedience alone, it is written, if you would enter my kingdom.3

  3. So, daughter, a horrifying incident that wrings my soul is what I heard had happened in Rome.4 There was a servant of the Lord whom God had endowed with many graces, among them that of prophecy. What do you expect? She obstinately refused to obey any longer. Alas! her directors came to doubt her salvation. So said a holy Card.5 Alas! the death of that servant of the Lord makes me fear she is saved. I assure you such a shudder ran through my bones that I prayed for her a whole night long. But! it is held for certain that she is in purgatory. However, they say, she suffers!!!6

  4. Daughter, let us obey blindly. Look, I am dying with the desire to go to America, but my Superiors said: no. Oh! I repeat, no, no! If we want love, we must obey. Let them call me ignorant, stupid, senseless. Oh! happy am I if they give me these titles for having obeyed.7

5. Courage; write to me always and try to do well as you always have. I hope that when this arrives the Superior will already have left for here to make the Holy Exercises. Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1 The one who should have set a good example: the Superior Elisa Corsini. Called to Piacenza for the Exercises, she telegraphed the Mother to say it was impossible to leave Maratea. Cf. L 130, n. 1. The Mother answered with a letter, but since it was undated the Superior thought it had been written in reply to an earlier letter of hers, before the telegram. Cf. L 15.8.78 to M.Rosa.

2 The Superior had written among other things: "I tried several times to leave, but the Delegate (a member of the governing Commission of the De Pino Institute) told me he would not allow it... and would have me stopped by the Carabinieri." The Commissioner's undue interference and the Superior's lack of clear ideas are evident.

3 Obedience alone, in the sense of full adherence to God's will. Mt 7:21-23.

4 A horrifying incident. One of the anecdotes told for moral ends by preachers of the time to reinforce doctrine and make a psychological impression on their hearers.

5 The Mother does not name the "holy Cardinal".

6 suffers, suffers greatly.

7 Daughter... obeyed. At the end of the instruction comes the forceful exhortation, backed by her personal witness.

She insists that she leave together with her fellow Sister, overcoming the obstacle put in her way.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Listen, you certainly cannot believe how sorry I am to hear that now they will not let you come.1 Do you know what you must do? Go to the steamer with Fabia and come here at once; I am already sure the Superior is the cause of it.2 Oh! if only I had never sent you there! How dreadful! so far away, and having to deal with some truly odd people.

2. Come in any case; I am expecting you. I am tired of hearing so many rumours and so much gossip; now yes, now no;3 indeed the poor Canon is doing everything for you. Oh! he is truly devoted to the Institute, not as the Superior says. I know he is working, writing.4 In short, you will hear what he has done. Goodbye, come soon. Sr. A. Fabia must repeat the subjects.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. Rosa

1. 2. If, however, Your Very Reverend Paternity has really decided to entrust this mandate to the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, I would not refrain from accepting it, and I would humbly ask you to observe the following points, which I make it my duty to set down here:

1. The religious must depend solely and fully on their Mother General, so that she may change any religious when she sees fit (in that case the journeys will be at the Institute's expense).

2. That every five years 4 Sisters may be recalled by the Mother, the journey to be at the Hospital's expense.

3. We wish to know the exact number of nursing religious required, noting that our Nurses need have no other skill than that of nursing the sick well, not that of being fit to teach school.2

4. We wish to know the annual allowance for each sister.

5. Whether the sisters will have only the care of the sick and the distribution of their food, or also the administration of the Hospital, and in that case under whose authority.

6. As for a change of habit, I cannot agree, because ours is very practical3 and convenient for nurses. His Holiness Pius IX too judged it most suitable. Considering also that Your Very Reverend Paternity told me that no religious congregation is yet there, I think it unnecessary to change the habit. Knowing no other style of religious dress in America, they will think ours is the one commonly worn, and all will be well.4

3. Awaiting your reply to this letter so that I may know how to proceed, I offer you my good wishes and profess myself your

Most devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno

Most Reverend Father,

One is allowing the Bishop of La Paz to make some change to the rules, to modify them, in short some small change.2 This is absolutely forbidden; indeed the article must be changed on this point to state that, both for the Constitutions and for our internal customs, no one may remove or add anything without the consent of the Major Superiors. My Father! did I not write to you that we cannot depend on anyone?

  2. Likewise Your Paternity tells me that the Sisters must promise to stay in La Paz for 10 years3 and moreover sign that they go willingly. Here too it seems to me that Your Paternity has not thought it through, or else does not yet know well the spirit of our Institute. So this promise Your Paternity must require from the Institute, that is, the Major Superiors.4 So I bind myself to send to La Paz 16 Sisters fit to serve and run the Hospital well; and if any had to return, either because she absolutely could no longer cope or because I thought fit to withdraw her, the journey would be at my expense.

  3. Listen, my Father, does it not seem to you that this contract of yours is all in their favour and nothing for us?5 So let us each give a little, shall we?6 Let us put six years as the obligatory period; what

do you say? If a sister died, the replacement to be made would of course be at the administration's expense.

4. I did not quite understand about maintenance. Here in Italy they pay us a salary or else a fixed amount,7 but we do not have to account to the administration for what is done.

5. Listen, Father: now, once we have reached agreement, I shall ask the Holy Father for his approval and submit to him everything that has been settled; that is my custom.8

6. The other small matters can be discussed in person; meanwhile today we began a triduum to St Francis, that he may obtain from God that everything goes well. Meanwhile bless me and believe me, with the greatest esteem and veneration, Your Paternity's

My daughter,

She has received the letters written during the voyage. She prays much, renewing with the 16 Sisters the offering of heart and will. She longs to be with them, but must be content to stay at the foot of Golgotha. She would like to see them in the wards serving and loving Jesus in the dear sick. She awaits news and joins them in spirit in the novena to the Child Jesus.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

  1. Just a line to tell you that I received all your letters during the voyage; the last is from Spain,1 where you tell me you suffered a good deal, but were well, cheerful and content, and that you have great courage. Oh! yes, this is all God's work, for dear Jesus has given you his gifts of strength and courage in the labours of so long a voyage.2

  2. I pray much, and every morning, tell the dear sisters, I offer the Lord your sixteen hearts together with your wills, that God the Father may do with them as he sees fit and give you strength, courage and living faith to do everything for him alone and want nothing for this earth; oh! how sweet it is to suffer for Jesus!3

  3. How often I have imagined myself among you, but I am not worthy; my wretchedness blocks my way from running swiftly to the summit of dear Mount Tabor, and I must always stay at the foot of Golgotha, to await the day of my departure to climb Calvary, and there alone where the beloved is.

  4. But! my dear daughters, I am only at the bottom of this mountain, eager to climb; but! who, who stands in the way? It is the barrier of my sins; it has dug itself in, and I struggle but cannot climb. Oh! Blessed are you if you get there! tell my Jesus that I am dying of

longing. Oh! you will find him, you will kiss him! and I, oh! what grief!!!4 Pray and say every day: "hear her and give her what she asks of you".

  1. Oh! I would like to see you, but!!! in the sweet wards beside the bed of Jesus, now dressing his wounds, now doing what he needs! And so he would give your hearts those sweet throbs of love; for every morning I ask him to consume you in himself.

  2. Oh! sweet Love! consume my dear creatures, and may I have all 16 with me in your kingdom for ever, for an eternity. I hope that only by the pure mercy of God can we go there.5

7. I await your letters anxiously; I assure you I count the days and hours; and I have written this so that you may have news of me before I have to answer the letters you will send me from La Paz.6 Courage; I am always with you; in the novena of the Child I shall try to hold him close in your hearts, as I am sure you will do the same for me.

Goodbye. The Lord bless you, and believe me always your more than

affectionate M. Rosa

1 Having left Genoa on 23 November 1878, they had called at Marseilles on the 25th and two days later at Bordeaux.

3 To the fundamental gifts of missionary spirituality, strength, courage, living faith, a spirit of sacrifice and exclusive love for Jesus, the 16 "sent ones" were to respond with the firm intention of living and acting for Jesus alone. The Mother offered herself with them, to give the Father living and docile instruments of his mercy.

5 I would like to see you... go there. She continues to sketch, with lyrical and evangelical concreteness, the profile of the FSA in her mission under every sky: moved by the love of Christ, she loves with the gentleness of His Heart and is consumed for Him in his kingdom for eternity. That is the homeland for her and her daughters.

6 She awaits news anxiously, and writes ahead of their arrival in La Paz so that they may feel her near. She wants to weave with them the net that unites them all in the heart of the sweet Saviour.

Thanksgiving for the Lord's blessings in the past year. Pope Leo XIII's goodwill towards the Institute. The Bishops' satisfaction and the goodwill of the people among whom we work. The Holy Mother's continual protection. New houses opened, including two in La Paz, Bolivia; an influx of new vocations. Recommendations to Superiors on love for the Mother, the financial management of their communities and the duty to send savings to the Mother House. Exhortations on observance.

A.M.F.

[Dearest daughters,]

1. The year now ending, 1878, sets before our eyes,

dearest sisters and daughters, the blessings which in the course of it we have received from the Lord. Oh! how numerous and great they are! One, and the most signal, is the goodwill with which his Vicar, the Supreme Pontiff happily reigning, Leo

XIII, looks upon our Institute. 1

Not only has he confirmed the gift of the house and vineyard at the Parrocchietta which the late Holy Father of holy memory made us at the end of his days, but at his own expense he has had that house restored. 2 We know that he greatly rejoices to see how quickly our Institute is spreading. This care which the Vicar of Jesus Christ takes for the growth of our Institute assures us that God takes pleasure in it.

2. The Bishops of the various Dioceses in which we have houses also show themselves well satisfied with the duties we perform there.

We also win the goodwill of the people among whom we work. A proof of this goodwill came from the people of Maratea, when the high-handedness of a Government Commissioner sought to send our teachers away and the whole population opposed it en masse with all the power in its hands. 3

3. But to what, dearest sisters and daughters, must we attribute so many blessings from Heaven? To the prayers which our Holy Mother continually offers at the Throne of the Lord. Yes, it is to her prayers that we owe the Institute's rapid growth: in this year now ending we have opened eleven houses, among which special mention must be made of the one we have founded in the new world, I mean in South America, where sixteen of our sisters have gone to take charge of two hospitals in the city of La Paz. 4

4. Ninety sisters have received the habit this year. So you see, dearest sisters and daughters, how many and how great are the blessings that call for our gratitude to the Lord who has deigned to bestow them on us.

5. But while in general we have reason to rejoice that in the houses of our Institute the fragrant sacrifice of observance of the Holy Rules is offered in thanksgiving to God for so many great blessings received from him, we are nevertheless obliged to deplore the failings in observance of some sisters.

6. In the first place, deplorable is the spirit of those superiors who show little affection for the Mother, who is, as it were, the centre and the sea of the Institute. These unfortunate superiors do not reflect that, just as a ray cut off from its centre goes out and a limb cut off from the heart dies, so they, having no affection for the Mother, are extinguished rays, dead limbs. The Holy Mother, seeing these unfortunate Superiors without affection for her first representative, cannot but abhor them, regarding them as apostates. 5

7. It is these unloving superiors who forget

that they are only the Mother's stewards in the Houses where she has placed them to represent her. And so they think themselves owners of the fees they receive for the schools and hospitals they run, and of the alms they receive; and, thinking themselves owners, they spend them as they please. In this way they become sacrilegious before

God, trampling on the vow of holy poverty, and become unjust and iniquitous towards the Institute.

8. Whereas good Superiors, who regard themselves only as the Mother's stewards, spend only what is necessary for the sisters' food and clothing and the other small expenses that arise day by day. And they do it with so thrifty an eye that they do not spend a cent on anything superfluous. These are the true lovers of the Institute; they are its true daughters, for they know that since the Mother House is where the Daughters of the Holy Mother are born, it should be helped by all the other Houses, which are its daughters; and so they are all eager and anxious to send it as much in savings as they can.

9. The Mother House is like the sea of the Institute; so, just as the limbs of the body are all concern that the heart be strong, since life depends on it, so all good superiors are anxious that the Mother House be helped and able to receive many postulants.

10. In the year just ended some hundred postulants have been received; but if there had been more help from the subordinate houses, how many more could have been accepted!

11. So while on the one hand we are grateful to those good superiors who show themselves true Daughters of the Holy Mother and zealous for the growth of her family, we urge those who are less zealous and loving to follow their example. And to help them manage well, at the end of this circular we set out the way in which they are to send in their accounts. 6

12. To the sisters in general we recommend first of all diligence in being punctual at the exercises of piety: meditation, Mass, communion, thanksgiving, prayers, the chaplet, 7 examination of conscience, the Holy Rosary; punctuality at common acts, at rising, breakfast, dinner, supper and recreation. Secondly we urge them to be industrious, carrying out well the tasks entrusted to them. Thirdly we urge them to see in their superiors the person of Jesus Christ, and so to love, respect and obey them, and above all never to speak to one another of their superiors' faults.

13. This, beloved sisters and daughters, is what the

Lord wants of us, to show ourselves grateful for the blessings God has bestowed on us in the year now ended and to be ready to receive new ones, so as to have the consolation of seeing our

Company 8 flourish for the glory of God and of the Holy Mother. Receive, as a sign of our motherly affection, the blessing with which we implore every good for you from the Lord. Thirteen have died. Pray for them.

[Gio. Batta Tornatore Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO] 9

Molinari wrote to M. Rosa on 29.1.1879: "... I was delighted to hear that the Father will be with you too..."

2 The corresponding letters are missing.

3 He would set out (trasportato).

She is in the greatest distress over Alessandro. She does not know where he is. She should make enquiries and write to her.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. I am in the greatest distress, because I know nothing more of

Alessandro. Where can he be? 1 You cannot believe how this thought distresses me; I fear he is in bed, and where? with those wretched women? Oh! what sorrow! 2

2. Go to the director and to the chemist's, 3 ask whether they know anything. I kept expecting him to come, since you told me he had come to Rome.

3. How is it? If it were not for his soul, I assure you I would never mention him again; but his soul? If he were to die? How dreadful! I feel torn apart.

4. If you learn anything, telegraph me and I shall be grateful. Goodbye, in haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. Send me one of those forms the benefactors sign, 5 even one already signed, so that I can see them; send it at once.

1 Cf. L 228

2 Ibid., para. 1

3 She should ask the Director of the Banca Industriale Subalpina or at the chemist's.

4 Cf. L 228, n. 6 and n. 9.

5 Forms by which benefactors pledged a contribution, usually monthly, to the FSA engaged in social work.

She is very busy. She too wants to meet her and be together.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A hasty line; believe me, I am so busy that I don't know whether I am coming or going. Oh! my God! You certainly cannot believe how busy I am; pray that I may get through it so as to come to you, and then we shall talk for a night and a day, on and on, never leaving each other. 1

2. What do you say? Is that it? Are you happy? Come! time flies and 5 months pass quickly; and then I shall be with you first; and afterwards you with me. 2 Goodbye, your

affectionate Sr. A. Rosa GATTORNO

1 Pray... each other. She went to Appignano on 16 February and left again on the 17th.

2 Come... with me. She had promised to have her come to Piacenza.

And then... but she should bear in mind that before that the Mother would go to her; and afterwards she would have to travel. The phrase I shall be with you first and afterwards you with me is playfully affectionate.

She has finished her work in Rome. After the audience with the Holy Father she will visit other houses: Capua, Naples, Cercola. She must also go to Loreto, in fulfilment of a vow. Sr. A. Benedetta is acting as her cook.

A.M.F.

My son, Dearest Carla,

1. I am writing in reply to yours of today with dear Noni's scribble enclosed. 1 Well done, nurse, don't go away; that way you keep us company and look after both of them for me, 2 for Carla too.

2. You, dearest Gaspare, for pity's sake I repeat, don't show Carla the sad letters; melancholy is poison to her, and to me it is a source of anxiety. 3

3. I shall come soon. Here in Rome I am done; 4 tomorrow I have the audience 5 and then I go to the Parrocchietta and I am done. I hope at the latest on Monday or Tuesday to leave for Capua, where I shall stay only two days, then about 6 in Naples and 2 in Cercola, and then at once I shall take the Foggia road, which is the shortest. I must go to Loreto in fulfilment of a vow, so I cannot avoid it.

4. As for Alessandro, don't be alarmed, because he can do nothing; if I chose to give him nothing, I am the owner, so all his fuss is useless. Don't be afraid; they are little bogeys worth nothing. 6

5. I shall make you laugh; you will hear from Sr. A. Benedetta. She is cooking all the time; I assure you it pains me to see her, and if it went on I would not like it; but if you saw her it is a real pleasure. She is in fine form, and so am I. When you have the carriage, think of going on nice outings, and so she can make up for being a cook and wear the secretary's uniform; I could do with a tasty morsel too. 7 So cheer up, let us be strong, for we shall have everything,

loving Jesus we have everything. I hear that Arnedos, that is Sr. A. Matilde, is at the Morte; I commend her to you; see that she gets well, consult the doctor; I commend her to you. 8 Goodbye affectionate M. ROSA

1 The letter has not been preserved.

2 Maria Adelaide's nurse, despite her husband's urging, kept putting off leaving for her family.

3 For Carla melancholy is poison; it makes me anxious about her health.

4 I have finished in Rome.

5 She had an audience with the Holy Father Leo XIII. Cf. L 236,2.

6 As for Alessandro: cf. L 228. It is useless for him to make a racket (battacare, a dialect word); don't be afraid, they are useless bogeys.

7 Both loved to joke.

8 The novice Sr. A. Matilde Arnedos was unwell and was being cared for in the infirmary house in Via della Morte. She commends her to him.

Various news. He should see to the journey of the Sisters going to Cotrone and collect the trunk at the station.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. In haste and it is late, because all day I am so busy you cannot imagine it; I get through things as fast as I can, but the long stairs tire me greatly.

2. Yesterday I had the audience and spoke to the Pope about Carla, the little doll and you at length; it was private, I was alone with him a good while!! how good he is! you will hear.

3. I would like to leave for Naples on Monday, but I still have endless things to do; I fear I cannot; at most it would be Tuesday. 1

4. The Father tells me 2 that for the timetable of those leaving for Cotrone you should do as you think best. See that it is the shortest, since it is so long, so that they do not suffer. 3

5. Today I expected a letter from you, but nothing; tomorrow at last the trunk leaves; be sure to send to the station [and] warn them not to break it open, because there is much in it liable to duty; have the duty paid so that it is not damaged! Have you heard the little doll's piano? Goodbye, yours. Has Sr. A. Sofia arrived? 4 yours, and a kiss to Carla and the little doll; I am your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Monday or Tuesday, 20 or 21 January.

2 Fr Tornatore had arrived in Rome on the 15th. Cf. L 232.

3 Cf. L 230,3.

4 Sr. A. Sofia, one of the Sisters assigned to Cotrone.

She entrusts him with some errands and tells him of her imminent visits to Capua and Naples. She expects to return to Piacenza at the end of February.

A.M.E

My son,

1. I have received yours enclosing the other from Florence; I would like you to tell me something about Sr. A. Matilde; see that she goes back to the Saint Anne House and take her away from the Morte, for there is nothing wrong with her, and I want them to look after her well. 1

2. Sr. A. Benedetta tells me she has received no address and does not know what you want.

3. Listen, have you given Albertazzi the money? If not, do it at once, for it is a disgrace; 2 the Father has told me everything. 3

4. I am toiling so hard to get finished 4 that I don't know how one could do more. On Monday or Tuesday, God willing, I shall leave for Capua, and after two days for Naples, where I shall stay as short a time as I can; and I hope that by the end of February I shall be done 5 and shall still arrive in time to taste the cold.

5. Goodbye; I enclose the key of the trunk, which was sent yesterday. Yours, and a kiss to the little doll and Carla; your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 235, n. 8.

2 Sante Albertazzi, the doctor attending the Saint Anne House.

3 Fr Tornatore had informed her of the situation in the house.

4 To get finished, to hurry and complete the work.

5 I shall be done, I shall have finished.

He should postpone the Sisters' departure for Cotrone. She leaves for Capua on the 21st.

A.M.F.

My son,

1. Just a line to tell you to postpone the departure of the sisters until I write to you again.]

2. Sr. A. Benedetta has her usual trouble and is vomiting. It must be my sins!

3. The day after tomorrow, God willing, I shall be in Capua.

4. Today I saw your brother Checchino, very kind; I did not see the others because I was not at home.

In haste, your

affectionate M. ROSA A kiss to all, goodbye.

1 Cf. L 230,3-5; 236,4.

She again asks for news of Alessandro.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Dear Daughter! Do you know that I still don't know where Alessandro is? 1 Oh! what sorrow! I cannot find peace! it is such that if I do not drive it away forcibly it tears me apart!

Is it possible that the lawyer knows nothing? 2 Goodbye; I must stop because I am about to leave. 3 Oh! how much work! Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 233.

2 Cf. L 229, n. 4.

3 She was to go to Capua.

Surprised by the telegram, she assures them that she has written. She too would like to see them again, but it is impossible.

A.M.F. My daughter,

  1. Your telegram surprised me today, and I hear that you have not received my letters. Oh, dear daughters, believe me, I wrote to you during the journey, although it was very painful and wearisome.1 Ah, yes! I too would very gladly see you. But what can be done for the moment? You have been there such a short time that it would seem foolish; don’t you agree?2 Enough.

I shall be in Naples on 3 February; pray hard for me and believe me, for all ages, your

affectionate M. Rosa

1 She wrote on 4 January from Naples. Cf. L 224.

2 The little community had arrived at Termini Imerese on 11 July 1878.

She has received news and has herself written during her visits to the houses. She will soon send the Circular. Advice on how to behave with the sick, in whom it is Jesus himself whom they nurse and care for. He is the only good; they must try to please him in everything so as to be together in his eternal glory, and pray, always united "in mind and heart".

A.M.F.

Dearest Daughters,

1. I have received the Superior's letter and hear that some of you have suffered, some more, some less. The last one I had, a few days ago, was from Rio de Janeiro, so by now you will be at your destination 1, all full of good will to edify those poor people and indeed the whole city of La Paz, which will be watching your actions with a thousand eyes. 2

2. I am sure and confident of success, because you made a solemn promise to Jesus, and every day I never forget to offer your 16 [hearts] to his Most Sacred Heart, thus united, with your wills. 3

3. I wrote you another letter shortly after you left, 4 so that you would find news of me, which will surely have been dear to you, as yours are to me; I long to receive the one that says: here we are, we have arrived!

4. Yes, daughters, since you left I can say I have not had a minute's rest, always travelling, during which I suffered a great deal, especially the journey from Piacenza to Rome, where I arrived by a miracle. 5 Now, as you see, I am visiting the hospital in Capua, where I shall stay until tomorrow evening, then Naples, and after the visit to Naples I am going to visit all our houses in the Abruzzi. 6 Pray for me. I am taking time to give you this little news,

which will please you. Soon I shall send you the Circular, which you will find fine, with so much good news. 7

5. Yesterday I received a paper describing your departure in detail and even giving all your names. Clearly the writer was well informed, wasn't he? 8 I am not writing to Father Rocchi because you will give him the news and greet him for me. I am waiting to write to him until I know he is somewhat settled and at rest. Tell us lots of things. I hope he will be pleased with your expedition and that everyone will admire your conduct in the hospitals.

7. Oh! We do everything for the glory of God and the good of our neighbour. 9 Let us see in those dear sick the person of our Jesus, dear redeemer! it is truly a sweet thought to tend Jesus! Blessed are you who can always have him before your eyes! Jesus in your heart, Jesus in bed, Jesus in all your duties! Oh! infinite sweetness! Without him there is nothing good or beautiful; with him we have everything and lack nothing; and to be sure of having him and doing all that pleases him, obey, and you will be sure of pleasing him and having him for eternity, and sure of running in God's true way, and one day we shall rejoice together in his glory.

8. Pray that I may have such good fortune, for only by his mercy can I enter there. Oh! how many iniquities! 10

9. Dear daughters, pray! And pray for a sinner who is so close to my heart that I cannot say more! 11

10. God bless you; always think of your poor

mother, whom you left not to be divided, but rather to be ever more united in mind and heart. Goodbye. I am yours for ever and ever affectionate M. ROSA Gattorno

1 The 16 Sisters reached La Paz on 20 January 1879.

2 In her longing she sees them thus: inspired by good will to "edify"

the poor and the whole city. To edify them above all by exemplary conduct that shows in deeds the consistency of a life offered to God and for love of him given to those they serve with a dedication that does not measure sacrifice, for love never says: enough!

3 She is sure of success, because all of them have committed themselves by a solemn promise to Jesus, giving him heart and will. A promise which she renews every day. Cf. L 207,2; 241, n. 3; 263, n. 6; 272, n. 6; 291,11; 299,3;

328, n. 8.

4 It is L 207 of 17 December 1878.

5 Especially that one: she suffered greatly, particularly on the journey Piacenza-

Rome.

6 After Capua (precisely S. Maria Capua Vetere, where the Sisters worked in the local hospital) she would go to other houses.

7 The circular was sent with a letter written on the same sheet. Cf. L 263.

8 A paper, the local newspaper reporting the departure and the names of the missionary Sisters.

9 We do everything... neighbour. This is the sole inspiring motive. From it the

Mother draws the teaching that follows, imbued with her personal experience of encountering Jesus in serving the sick.

10 Pray... iniquities. She concludes the teaching by stressing the eschatological dimension of life as the pure gift of the Father of mercies to her, full of iniquities.

11 ... a sinner. The reference to Alessandro seems clear. Cf. L 226;

233; 239; 245,5; 246,4.

She is pleased with the good news. She urges observance.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. You cannot believe how dear your letter was to me, always bringing me happy news of your well-being and the peace you enjoy; 1 may God keep it for you always; and you will always have it, provided you observe your holy Rules; if you have observance, you certainly have everything. 2

Many greetings to all, and believe me your

affectionate M. ROSA Greet M. for me! 3 The address: Cav. Manari [Antonio], Via Lucina No. 17

1 Happy news of your good health and the peace of the community.

2 Observance of the code of life is the sure track that eases the community's journey in fulfilling God's will.

3 M.: perhaps Manari, whose address she copies. He was the adviser who in

Rome helped deal with the works' administrative problems.

She encloses the receipt for the parcel she has sent. She will have to stay at least 15 days.

A.M.F.

Dearest Son,

1. A hasty line to enclose the receipt; you will see what lovely things you will find, how many toys for the little doll; 1 I shall bring the others with me. I shall send the carpet in the next few days.

2. I am so busy I don't know how to breathe. Certainly I cannot stay less than 15 days; Sr. A. Benedetta will write to you this evening.

Goodbye, yours, and warm wishes to all

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The toys for the little doll, little M. Adelaide, were a gift from Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega.

She is pleased with the news of the new house. She will make arrangements with the applicant.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am answering yours at once. 1 I hear the good news about the house we are to take; God be praised. When he writes to me I shall reply and we shall come to an agreement, and I shall send him the teacher too. 2

Goodbye. I am really tired. Your affectionate M. ROSA

2 When he: the Vicar Forane Giuseppe Bartolini. On 3.1.1879 he had already asked the Mother for three Sisters for an orphanage to open in June 1879. Cf. Register 1876-1881.

She has learned that Alessandro is in Rome, but cannot accept fear as the reason for his silence, for she has let him know several times that she forgives him. She orders her not to sit up with the sick. She asks for prayers for her son's conversion.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. A line to tell you I received yours and the other one. 1 Now I hear he is in Rome; I shall write to him; 2 but you must know that I have sent word several times that I forgive him, and not only that but bless him. And yet how can he say he fears my anger? it is quite otherwise. 3

2. Oh! dear daughter, I hear you have sat up many nights. 4 Ah! I do not approve of this at all. It would be one thing if it had been just one night, but there have been so many!

3. I tell you in virtue of holy obedience that I forbid it; I allow one at most, if it is something truly extraordinary. 5 Do you understand me? So I tell you that you must look after yourself. How are you?

4. Now I am writing to him. 6 Ah! what an unhappy Mother! Truly it is my sins that make things go so, and what a dreadful thing to think of that son!

5. I no longer know what to say: only prayers can obtain for me that he be converted, at last become a good Christian and save his soul. 7

6. I assure you it is so cruel a matter to have to think about. Ah! Yes! My Jesus, your cross is sweet, but to think that it is a son who causes it, for fear that he may be lost... Goodbye, your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The two letters: of 29 and 17 January.

2 She wrote that he was in Rome and gave the address received from a friend of his:

poste restante, for correspondence.

3 She cannot believe his silence is due to fear, for he knows well that she has not only forgiven him but blesses him.

4 In the L of 17.1.1879 she wrote that she had sat up with a patient for three nights and would go on "as much as she can" because she wanted to please everyone.

5 The prohibition is firm. The office of superior cannot be reconciled with serving the sick in that way.

6 I shall write to him, to Alessandro.

7 The Mother has faith in the power of prayer.

She thanks her for the Sicilian sweets sent to Piacenza. She would like to see her dear daughters again, but for now it is impossible. She asks for prayers and urges her to carry on courageously, always united to God.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to keep my word: here I am in Naples, in the midst of an abyss of business.

2. Carlottina writes that the box of sweets that arrived in Piacenza 20 days ago was absolutely delicious. The Father says the same, 1 and they arrived in excellent condition despite being so long in transit.

3. Thank you, then, a thousand thanks! Oh! To know you are so near 2 and not be able to embrace and see you truly grieves me, I assure you. I am staying here until the 6th. If you want to write to me, if you need me to answer you, just tell me.

4. You will have heard of the death of poor Countess Trotti. Have prayers said for her; and I also ask you to pray for the conversion of a sinner; have the girls pray. 3

5. I hope you are all well. Greetings to all the sisters; and you, my dear daughter, courage and strength, always united to God; try to remain in his presence in everything, and so you will draw light to guide the little flock. I am so busy that I must stop.

Goodbye, your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Fr Tornatore. Cf. L 232.

2 so near. Compared with Piacenza they were near, since by sea the journey was relatively short.

3 Pray. Countess Trotti had died on 2 January '79; she also asked for prayers for Alessandro's conversion. Cf. L 245,5; L 241,9.

She has received the accounts and the money. If possible, she should keep the postulants a while longer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your letter with the money inside, and the account too.

You did well to send the money to me; always do so, because that way I am spared having it sent to me.2

2. Have you already sent the two postulants to Piacenza? If you have not sent them yet, I think you could keep them for a little longer;3 otherwise, if they are a trouble to you, send them to

Piacenza.

Goodbye, I am in a hurry; greet the sisters for me. Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is deduced from Santina's letters of 17 and 29 January.

2 She did well to send her the surplus; that way she avoids having it sent back from Piacenza.

3 She refers to the postulants.

She tells her she is going to Rome. She is trying to obtain a piano for her.

A.M.F.

My dear Daughter,

1. I hear about the cook; if you see she is no good, send her here. As for what you have, if you want to send it to me in Rome, where I shall stay 15 [days].2

2. As for the piano, be a little patient;3 I am leaving Sr. A. Ulderica4 in charge of seeing whether she can find one like hers to send you in Bovino, spending about 100 lire, so that you can give lessons. Goodbye. Tomorrow, God willing, I shall be in Rome. Your affectionate M. ROSA

I shall send you another when this one is here.5

1 The date is inferred from what she says about her return to Rome.

2 There is no corroborating information to understand this paragraph properly.

3 As for the piano, she had to be patient. The Sister had complained to her several times because she could neither practise nor give lessons.

4 She would have given the task of finding it to Sr. A. Ulderica Tazioli.

5 She refers to the transfer of the cook.

Instructions about two Sisters. She asks for prayers for the conversion of a sinner and for her journey.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Send the Sister straight back to Nizza, where she was;2 as for Sr. A. Giusta, tell her that as soon as she is well she will certainly go; if only she had stayed put the other time.3

2. For the moment I cannot send any nurse because I have none; when I return to Piacenza I shall send you one.

3. I am very glad you have paid the rent; I thank God for it.

4. Pray for me and for a sinner, that he may be converted,4 and that God may give me strength to finish this journey. Goodbye, your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Cf. L 223,3.

3 The Sister wanted at all costs to go to Piacenza. The Mother had had to agree, provided she was taken to the infirmary in via della

Morte. Cf. L 223 and 227. Evidently she was then in Genoa.

4 The sinner is her son Alessandro. Cf. L 241,9; 245,5; 246,4.

She has received the letters. She urges trust, courage and living for Jesus alone.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. A hasty line to tell you I have received your letters.2 For pity's sake, be at peace and try not to distress yourself, because everything that happens is always for our good; besides, you must know that what I tell you is always for your good and that I desire nothing else than to see you holy.3

2. So courage, onward, and all for Jesus. Love him alone very much and live for him.

God bless you; and believe me always your

affectionate M. ROSA I am leaving4 your

1 This L is from February, as shown by the correspondence of Sr. A. Genoveffa

Molinari, superior of the Bovino Community, which the Mother visited together with Fr Tornatore in February 1879. AFSA, CsIM - 1879.

2 Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli wrote to her often, and so did the Sisters.

3 Cf. L 224.

4 I am leaving. Cf. L 252, n. 2.

She sends her the letter appointing her Superior of the Lugo community. Advice on the new office.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. I enclose this letter of obedience2 for the sisters; as soon as it has been read, you will be Superior of the Lugo House.

2. Try to do as the others did: be observant and punctual, and try to give the best example you can to the sisters and the girls; watch over the finances and provide the sisters with what they need, and charity for the sick.3 In short, be a true Mother.4

May the Lord bless you, while in my dear Crucified

affectionate Mother Sr. A. Rosa G.

1 The year is missing, but the letter is clearly from 1879.

2 Sr. A. Irene had been in Lugo since the start of the school year (October 1878). Cf.

L 160. Now she sends her official appointment as Superior.

3 ... charity for the sick. Attention and care were not to be withheld from the community's "jewels".

4 In short: here is the genuine profile of the FSA superior.

She had to leave Bovino without being able to express her gratitude in person. She also apologises to his wife for not receiving her, as she was suffering from a severe migraine.

Most Illustrious Mr Mayor,

1. Very sorry to have to leave Bovino2 without the honour of speaking to you and expressing my most heartfelt gratitude for all that Your Most Illustrious Lordship kindly does for the poor Daughters of Saint Anne; I hope their cooperation will satisfy Your Lordship in what they give3 that most worthy population through their teaching and by helping, if need be, the poor sick.4

2. Meanwhile I humbly ask you to obtain from your excellent wife a charitable indulgence for my not having been able to receive her on Sunday,5 forced to it by a headache; (but for) which it would have been a pleasure for me to tell her in person what I say above.

Please accept my respects, while, full of esteem for Your Most Illustrious Lordship, I remain

Your most humble and devoted [Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno]

1 The date is assumed from the chronology of her visit to Bovino and from the superior Genoveffa Molinari's remark to M. Rosa: "the mayor was a little displeased that you had not gone to visit him". L 16.2.79, CsIM, 1879.

2 She had arrived on the 9th and left again on 11 February. Cf. L 250,2.

3 nel dare: for what they give.

4 and by helping: in case of need, in caring for the poor sick.

5 Sunday, 9 February.

She describes her latest movements. She is tired and longs to be back in Piacenza. She commends Carla, whose time to give birth is near. She has sent a basket and a sack.

A.M.F. My son,

1. A line from Acquaviva, where I am staying only until 3 tomorrow; then, God willing, in the evening I shall be in Loreto, where I shall stay only a few hours, and on Sunday at noon I shall be in Appignano.2 If God gives me strength, on Tuesday evening I shall be in Lugo, on Wednesday night in Ferrara.

2. Oh! when shall I be able to write to you from Ferrara! Then I shall feel near.3 I assure you I cannot sleep, such is the distress I feel.4

3. I commend Carla to you, as her delivery approaches, and since it is a boy it comes 20 days early.5 Do not leave her; find out who is a good midwife for the baby, and tell Albertazzi if you decide to engage him. Tell him to come and see her every day and always to leave word where he can be found, if he is doing everything. In short, try to have everything ready, because I have it in my head that it will happen in a moment.

4. Tell her to be cheerful, for a saint, indeed two, to whom I was fortunate enough to speak about her,6 told me she will have a very happy delivery, and soon, very well. I have some water7 for her to drink.

5. Sr. A. Benedetta saw one of them go into ecstasy. Oh! how she wept together with Sr. A. Speranza!8 What beautiful souls.

6. Oh! dear Gaspare, what things we have seen!

Now I am a little tired, but what can you do? I really see that one cannot avoid coming to these houses.

7. Goodbye; today a sack and a basket are being sent from here, in which we shall also put all our things so as not to camatare9 so much.

Greet all the sisters for me, Sr. A. Nazarena, and you, Carla, little doll, I embrace you and am your affectionate M. ROSA

8. A sister from Florence, coming from Foligno, will have arrived, and I hope her relatives will have come to fetch her; see that she goes.

1 This L was included among those of January, but its content makes it clear that it is from February.

2 Appignano (Macerata); she arrived there on Sunday 19 February.

3 When she is finally in Ferrara she will feel she is close to returning.

4 She is now very tired from the journeys and the visits to the houses.

5 She had been told that Carlotta would have a boy, and she knew that boys generally are born before the expected time.

6 Two persons reputed to be holy had reassured her. She had met them in Naples.

7 Holy water.

8 Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega and Sr. A. Speranza Volpini had been moved.

9 Camatare, an incomprehensible word.

She invites her to a meeting in Bologna, where she will be passing through on the 22nd.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Just a line to let you know that, as I cannot come,2 you and Sr. A. Leopoldina will join those from Bagnacavallo and come to meet me on Saturday the 22nd in Bologna, in the room Sr. A. Domenica already knows.3

2. Wait for me all together in that room;4 we shall have lunch together and stay there until evening, when I shall take one train and you another, each to her destination.

Dearest daughter,

1. It seems impossible that you keep letting the mail boats go without sending me news of yourself and the sisters,1 and I assure you I am in constant anxiety when I see no letters from you. It is now 20 days2 since I received one, and I say: "what is my daughter Giuseppina doing? Does she think that the one left behind does not feel the emptiness and loss of not being able to see you?"

2. Oh! Daughters! those in Italy certainly do not cost me as many prayers as you do. Oh! no! I can truly say so! And why do you never write to me?3 Perhaps it has been otherwise with you: out of sight, your heart has grown distant! Oh! what a thought this is for me! Come, be a little more prompt in writing to me.4

3. And then I say: "Oh! What can they be doing?" While they left me their hearts and wills, I am faithful and every day I offer them to

God and hold you in the heart of Jesus, and I pray my dear Crucified never to let you escape and always to keep you within him.5

4. Oh! Sweet dwelling, where nothing is found but love and joy. You who long for joy, hold fast to him and in him you will find love and joy. Love that gives every kind of sweetness!6

5. I hope you will tell me lots of things, as I long for that. Goodbye7, and remember that [I am] your mother; it is true I am poor and ugly, yet I shall repeat to you: "I am your mother"! Even poor children, even if they have an ugly, poor mother, still love her, because she is their mamma, and prefer her to any princess or noblewoman on earth. Enough.

6. I want to drive from my mind the dreadful thought, which so afflicts me, that you may have forgotten me, or that your hearts are not attached!!! No, No! I see these are sad thoughts and I want to drive them away.

7. Listen, when you write, always remember to include greetings to our Bishop, and write to him directly, which he will appreciate; please do so.8

8. By now you will have received the news that we have been definitively approved by bull; so now we are like all religious bodies and no one can say anything any more, except that we are true Daughters of the Apostolic and Roman Church.9

9. Stand firm in the holy Rules, for now they are a precept and no longer something changeable but binding;10 so, observance, for by it we shall become holy and one day all be blessed in Heaven. And if you pray that God may have mercy on me, I shall come too. So courage! a brief suffering for an eternal joy.

10. So write to me, for I am truly anxious. Write to me, and a lot, do you understand?

11. I greet you all and wish you a thousand blessings from Heaven, and believe me yours for ever and ever.

Affectionate M. ROSA

P.S. In a few days the case of scotch cloth, muslin, tibet and soap will leave.11

1 The mail boats. Cf. L 291,2 and n. 2.

2 Since early May.

3 Why do you never write to me? The news received dated from 7 March.

Too long a time and too many unknowns for her mother's heart.

4 She tries to find a reason for that unbearable silence.

5 Her thought runs from the moment of farewell and promise (cf. L 207,2)

to the unknown present.

6 Oh! Sweet dwelling... sweetness. The thought of Jesus' love prompts an ardent and urgent exhortation.

7 Goodbye. Perhaps she meant to finish and left the letter incomplete. On taking it up again she returns to the pain caused by that long silence and looks for other reasons for it.

8 Cf. L 272,7. 9 Cf. L 291,6.

10 Something changeable: that can be altered as we please

11 Cf. L 291,3.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. I hear all you tell me, and I am very sorry you are not yet well, indeed fully recovered. Oh! how it grieves me! Take care of yourself; remember that by doing so you practise holy Obedience, do you understand?1

2. The Canon is free; let him do as he pleases; it means there will be no lack of occasions to come [with] postulants to accompany.2

3. How did the business with Buonacursi go? Oh! how sad; is he no longer in Pistoia? and whom is his daughter with?3

4. Let everyone say what they like about the sisters, as long as they are well.4 The one you sent me is almost cured. Poor creature! Tell me, did you never do anything for her, ointments or the like? I gave her an ointment and it has done her so much good that she has almost nothing left.5

5. Thank you for the wine, a thousand thanks. Let Bianca write to the Father too.6

Goodbye, yours for ever affectionate M. ROSA

2 The Canon, as usual, was stalling. He had asked her to write to the Mother: "do not take it amiss, he cannot now, he will be able to come in June."

3 Bonaccorsi, a benefactor who supplied the house with wood and coal, had separated from his wife and moved with his daughter to Florence. Letters of Sr. A. Crocifissa to M. Rosa: 10, 19 and 23 May 1879.

5 Cf. L 293,1. 6 Fr Tornatore.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. In haste, please send me at once the sister whose name I don't remember, you know, the one you leave in your place when you come here and whom you know we said1 would make a superior, the one I told you to keep ready for me because she would come later, that is, I would call for her; now, do you understand?

2. Send her to me at once, as soon as possible; I need her.

3. I have received yours and hear all is well. Patience about Bonaccorsi.2 God will see to it.

Two Sisters will arrive. She should train one for the kitchen and the other for nursing. The Sister coming from Rome she should keep in order to test her vocation and her will to amend. She expects Canon Biagini for Saint Anne's feast.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you the two sisters you ask for: one is old and strong and is to do the cooking, the other is for nursing; so they will get some training with you and then we shall send them to other places where I cannot send novices.1 Listen, try to train them for me, because then I shall take them back.

2. Listen, one will reach you from Rome; test her well, for this is the last trial I am giving her, and then she will have to be sent away. Her bad qualities are: she is a liar and deceitful, and one must be very careful with the sick because she tells lies; I say this so that she may be watched and not do harm.2 Do you understand?

3. I hear about the Canon. Very well; for my part I am delighted and have nothing more to wish for; I only long for the Lord to keep him in good health and for him to come here with good Angiolina, your farm manager's wi-fe; tell him.3 Give him my warmest greetings; I expect him for Saint Anne's feast, he must spend it with us. Yes! Let him come.

Dear daughter, look after your health, which matters so much to me. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

2. As for the vineyard, half of it is still yours; I have already given the matter to Cavaliere Manari, who will deal with it, and let us hope it ends well;2 meanwhile let us pray. Goodbye, I am in a hurry.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line. To train this sister, the older one, I should like you to teach her to cook; she is strong; here it was always laundry and the sick;1 and the other for the sick, for now other.2 Yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA
