Educational advice and spiritual exhortations.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am sending you a form for the statement of accounts;1 I should like you to keep a little closer watch on the orphanage.

2. From certain reports I hear that the girls are somewhat neglected and that you do not agree among yourselves in giving punishments.2 You must support one another; when you give a punishment it must be upheld, and likewise when the others punish a girl, you must support them.3

3. If something seems wrong to you, you must tell them privately. So, for pity's sake, this is an important point.4

4. I do not want you to be alarmed by these remarks of mine; they are only meant to help you all do your duties better.5

5. I commend Sr. A. Sempliciana to you. Help her with the needlework so that she does not worry, and I should like her not to fret too much.6

6. You too, I want to see you braver, and in your little crosses do not be dismayed, but be strong and carry this dear cross with love and resignation.

7. All for Jesus, a brief suffering for an eternal joy.7 I am sending you the form for the half-year accounts. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 For the half-yearly statement.

2 You lack a common approach in correcting the girls when you assign punishments.

3 You must support one another. You especially must accept the punishment assigned by the Sisters.

4 So take care: this is an important educational rule.

5 It had happened before. Cf. L 275.

6 Cf. L 285,2.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Seeing that you are suffering too much and that I shall not come until the end of June, I have thought of sending you to Piacenza, so that you can recover a little.2 Courage! Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

She should keep watch on the sister on trial. She will send the belongings of the other two.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, I urge you to keep a close eye on the sister who was brought to you from Rome, and if you see she is not behaving, you must write to me at once and then send her to me straight away. Enough, I am telling you what to do.1

2. As for the Sisters' belongings, I shall send them to you as soon as the washing is done.2 One even left her shifts unfinished, but I shall send them.

3. The news you give me is very dear to me.3 Listen, the Sister will be sent home, because everything has been tried. It means she must be sent away, mustn't she?4

Goodbye. In great haste, your affectionate M. ROSA

She is pained by the long, inexplicable silence. She should accept postulants, whom she can later bring to Piacenza and so have the comfort of seeing her. She also hopes for financial help from her in such hard times. She longs for many Bolivian vocations to spread knowledge of and honour to Saint Anne. She has heard about the war: she should not worry; Saint Anne will always protect and defend her Daughters.

A.M.F.

Dearest daughter,

1. How your very long silence pains me: My God, what can it be, are you ill perhaps?1 For pity's sake, do not let the packet boats go by without writing to me, do you understand?2

2. How are the Sisters, have they settled in well? Listen, I should not like you to be like some, out of sight, out of mind; no, no, I will not believe it, because my Giuseppa cannot lessen the affection she bears in her heart for her poor mother, can she? Yes! It cannot be otherwise.

3. Oh! I wish the years would pass like the flight of birds, for then I would have the comfort of seeing you.

4. Yes, my daughter, try to accept postulants, then you can bring them here to me3 and Holy Mother Saint Anne will be well pleased too.

5. I hope you will also be able to help me in certain needs, for God alone could say how much my poor head suffers having to think hard about so large a family in such hard times.4 Oh! what troubles, my dear; if you could see a little of what goes on here you would certainly pity me. For pity's sake, think of your mother.

6. Listen, the papers here report everything you send me in the La Paz papers.5 I long for more Sisters to go there, as Father Rocchi tells me we shall soon be called to other places in La Paz, that is, in Bolivia, and then I can send you a few more Sisters for yourself.

7. How sad not to have letters from you, you will surely not believe it; tell the Sisters too to write to me a little; and please write to the Bishop.6

8. I enclose a letter from Gaspare; if you need anything, apply to him and he will do everything for you; he has already sent you the scotch cloth and muslin, and I also had him put in a piece of tibet for the scapulars, because I thought you would like it and perhaps you had forgotten.7

9. I wish God would send a hundred postulants, so that there too we might have a great band of Daughters of Saint Anne, and the Holy Mother might be loved and honoured in La Paz as well by a great number of Daughters.

10. Oh! blessed are you who for Jesus have crossed the sea and set out on a fine road to holiness, and more, ready to endure martyrdom.8

11. How distressing to know there is war in those parts;9 we are praying that it may soon end and you may be at peace; it is true I am told it is far from La Paz, but still I am much troubled. But do not worry, for the Saint will help you and will not let you suffer in the least; she will always protect her daughters and defend them for all ages until the end of the world, without their being troubled in the least.

12. You will have received the decree of definitive approval of the Institute, haven't you?10

13. Tell the sisters I send them warm greetings, and Father Rocchi and everyone; and you, receive a thousand affectionate greetings from one who holds you in the Heart of Jesus and calls herself for ever

your affectionate M. ROSA

She needs her. She should get the examinations brought forward to mid-July and leave soon.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. What will you say about my not having written to you again? My God! My occupations and labours are beyond belief.

2. The purpose of these two lines is to tell you that I absolutely need you for 26 July; so hold the examinations at once; try to hold them in mid-July and have everything finished by the 20th.

3. Come at once, even alone; just write to me four or six days beforehand and I shall tell you whom to come with.

4. If this letter of mine finds the Superior still there,1 you can tell her that I want you to hold the examinations by 15 or 20 July. Do you understand?

5. You can give the heat as the reason, a true reason. They might only want school to reopen about 15 days earlier; very well, that will be done; indeed you can promise it.2 That settles it. So by the 20th at the latest you must leave Bovino, July, that is.3 Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The Superior Sr. A. Genoveffa Molinari.

2 If they allowed the examinations to be brought forward, the authorities might require the school to reopen earlier. That can be accepted.

3 The permission requested was not granted. Sr. A. Agnese left for Piacenza on

10 August.

Warnings about a Sister. She should send a Sister to Gualdo Tadino.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen, before sending me the Sister you should have told me something or at least warned me. Enough, it is done now.1

2. As for the other, watch her well, for she does this everywhere: three days good and then she deceives with all her wickedness. Gossip is her daily bread, and so she does harm among the sick, and often... be careful.2

4. Listen, it is only a few lire from Pistoia to Gualdo; I hope you will give her them, won't you? Altogether, third class, it is 15 [lire], I think. I long to see you and talk with you.

Goodbye. Greetings to all; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had sent a Sister in difficulty to the Mother House without prior notice.

2 Cf. L 305,2; 310,1.

3 In two days the Superior in Florence is to send a Sister to Foligno. It is good to write to her; she has already been told.

She is pleased with the news received. Blessings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Blessed be God that peace and calm have returned among you.1 I wish you a thousand blessings, so that you may always be so.

Goodbye, I am immensely busy; your affectionate M. ROSA

My daughter,

1. I hear what you tell me about the sister.1 Very well. Now you should send a good one, of long-standing vocation, to Florence for nursing, which they need so badly; I cannot tell you how great their need is; if you need one, I shall send you one from here.

My daughter,

1. I am answering yours by return of post. To accept the girls you can reply as follows:1 1st They must pay; one must see whether they are boarders, in which case a large fee is needed, [or] day pupils; but this fee must serve to support another sister; 2nd because I cannot allow more work to be added, as you are already too tired.2

2. So, depending on the place, which you know, you will see what can be asked. I would say not to ask less than 8 or 10 francs a month (for day pupils). For boarders you will have to ask either 40 or 30, depending on the instruction.

your affectionate M. ROSA

She has written to the Bishop. She should go to him and explain the state of the work and her wish to come to Piacenza to confer with the Mother. She shares her sorrows and awaits her. Before leaving, she should get the Marchioness to pay the boarding school's expenses.

A.M.F.

Dearest Daughter,

1. I have just finished reading yours1 and am replying at once, and I am also writing to Mgr to tell him that I place everything in his hands and he should do whatever he thinks fit, that I am and always shall be content and approve everything, and shall count myself fortunate to obey him;2 and that I am writing to you to go and receive his orders and tell him frankly everything you are going through and how she treats you.3

2. And say to him: "Excellency, I should like to go to the Mother in Piacenza to tell her everything in person and meanwhile to find a little relief; I cannot go on. If Your Excellency agrees, I shall try to be accompanied by a postulant, and then for the return journey the Mother will give me a sister, as some are due to leave for Sicily, and she can keep me company".

3. Be of good heart, my dear daughter. Listen, I wish I could take all your sorrows on myself and relieve you, and so make you a little happier;4 but be of good heart, for it will all end and you will see that you will be content, and you will come, and we shall spend a little time together and there will be no more troubles for you.

4. Listen, before you let the Marchioness know you want to leave, tell her, by fair means or foul as you think best, to pay you,

because you have incurred expenses and have money to pay; that is no lie, the money has to be paid; and be firm; so before she knows you are leaving,

5. Do you understand? from now on do this: take a lot, and all in her name. What do you say? Do you agree?

6. You long to see me, and I? Oh! I would have too much to say; I long for it. Goodbye, because I want to post this. I am your

affectionate M. ROSA

2 She relies on the mediation of Archbishop Guglielmo Sanfelice to resolve the problem of the "S. Teresa" orphanage, caused by the "authoritarian" way Marchioness Laura Balbi Caracciolo ran the work and by her improper interference in the Sisters' community. Cf. L 135,2-3 and n. 4.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This is a good novice; I am sending her to you to get her used to things, then I shall take another.1 Thank you for the cheese and everything;2 for pity's sake, I am unwell and so busy that I really don't know what to do. Pray for me, and I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 She entrusted her to her to train and prepare her for a future mission in another house.

2 Cf. L 319,3.

She calls her to Piacenza.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. In haste: yes, come, come, for I long for you; I am staying put.2 Goodbye, I await you. Yours, yours, yours; greetings to the Sisters, telegram style, registered. All right?

Affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context. Cf. L 320.

2 I am here in Piacenza.

She asks for approval and the pastoral blessing to begin the educational work with the children in the Bellagio Infant School.

Most Reverend Excellency

1. As we have been called to an Infant School in your Diocese, in the town of Bellagio, before going there I ask Your Most Reverend Excellency for permission and your pastoral blessing, so that the Sisters who are to begin this mission may have from Heaven the protection of blessed God. Please grant them the graces they need to guide those innocent souls well.

2. Awaiting a reply from you raising no objection, as I am sure it will,1 I prostrate myself at your feet imploring your Pastoral blessing, while I remain with all veneration Your Most Reverend Excellency's

Most humble and devoted Servant Sr. A. Rosa GATTORNO

1 The Bishop replied on 9 July 1879: "I not only permit their coming to this Diocese of mine, but thank you for it with all my heart". AFSA, CvIS, F 58.

The three FSA chosen by the Mother for the Infant School reached Bellagio on 17 July 1879.

She should promptly replace a sick sister, transferring her to Foligno.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Send Sr. A. Beniamina1 to Gualdo Tadino at once. Oh!

that house this year is truly a curious business; and that Sr. A. Emma, as I already foresaw, will have done penances and so she is very weak;2 try to take her to Foligno, for she is a healthy sister; it is just whims.3

2. So see to it quickly; please send her at once, for pity's sake, and you will see. Goodbye.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Sr. A. Beniamina Baraldi.

2 pigra: weak. She was weakening herself by doing penances.

3 The Superior, Sr. Restilde Colombo, had asked her for another Sister,

because Sr. A. Emma Piccinini had never been well since she arrived. The

Mother is convinced that her poor health is caused by self-imposed penances of not eating enough.

She urges her to be patient and forgive. She should take heart, be prudent and magnanimous.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. The work is beyond measure; now, in one of your letters you tell me that if you saw them insult you or the sisters you would show them.2 No, Jesus did not teach us that: turn the cheek to receive another blow!!!3

2. The other letter comforted me greatly, and I hear that everyone is well disposed; praise be to God;4 but you must not let the sisters hear you say that what people do is for political motives; no, we must think that everyone acts with a right intention, after all.5

I leave you in my dear Jesus Crucified.

Your affectionate M. ROSA

3. All is well: the accounts, the Vows for all; keep everything with you; in a few days you will have the Superior.6

1 The date is inferred from the context and content.

2 On 20 June she had complained strongly of the arrogance and malice of the Mayor, who had "scolded her" in the street for sending away the teacher.

3 Mt 5:39 "...if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also...".

4 The other letter (of 29 June) comforted me because many people are on your side.

5 The Superior, however, had no confidence; she was not convinced of the good intentions of those who sided against the Mayor.

6 She had closed the first half-year's accounts and could keep the cash surplus. On 17 June she had given a favourable opinion on admitting the

Sisters to renewal of Vows and had asked to be relieved of the office of Superior.

She will send the document requested. She urges prayer for the resolution of a deplorable situation.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in reply to your two letters.2 If the sisters stay, I shall send you [what you ask] about what you tell me concerning the Canon.3

2. Oh! My God! Let us pray very, very much; at once have the whole month you are keeping for the Saint dedicated to this, that she may remedy so dreadful a thing, and likewise to the Sacred Heart.4 He is powerful and will certainly do everything.

3. I hope the Superior in Florence has sent you the monstrance.5

Goodbye, yours, yours for ever affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 One of 26 June 1879, the other n.d.

3 If the Sisters going to Pistoia stay longer in

Piacenza, I can send you what you mention... Canon Biagini wanted to amend the will, replacing Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni's name with that of another religious and adding further details. Perhaps the Mother wanted her lawyer to prepare the draft.

5 The Sister to whom she had entrusted it had left it behind in Florence.

She has always answered her letters. She should drive away melancholy and press on courageously. She has much work and is very weak.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I cannot understand why you complain that I do not write to you; I sent you a letter by the Superior;1 I never let your letters go unanswered. It must be your melancholy that makes it seem so.

2. Come now, we shall soon see each other; I see the days flying by and soon I shall be with you and you can pour out your heart as much as you like.2 Be cheerful, for pity's sake; melancholy is the devil's net, which he casts and then!3

3. Oh! no, my daughter is certainly not like that; she belongs wholly to Jesus and wants to live, die and toil for him alone. So courage.

4. I shall write no more; I leave you to imagine how much I have to do, and I assure you it is unbearable, as I am so weak I cannot stand.

Goodbye. Greetings to all the sisters; I allow them all to renew their Holy Vows,4 and I remain yours for ever

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The Superior of one of the Naples houses, Sr. A. Speranza Volpini, had gone to Piacenza.

2 You can pour out your heart as much as you like. You will have all the time you need to tell me what is in your heart.

3 ... is the devil's net, which surrounds and then takes hold of its poor victims.

4 She allows all to renew their vows on the feast of Saint Anne.

For three months she has had no letters. She should write and send news to set her mind at rest. In Italy requests for new houses and the influx of postulants continue. She will not call the Superiors together because she cannot meet the expense. Greetings and instructions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I am now sending this letter to the Consul for him to forward to you, so as to get news of you, for I am in the greatest anxiety; for pity's sake, write to me. It is now three months since I have heard anything; what pain!1 Since you arrived in [La] Paz I have received three letters. For pity's sake, tell me whether you have received my letters and how many; how many sheets I have sent you! The scotch cloth has been sent as well; the soap could not be.

2. I am writing and I feel really ill; I am in such agitation as you would not believe, even though my God gives me strength, and meanwhile this wretched human nature imagines all sorts of things! Are they ill? Can they not get what they need to live? How is observance going?3

3. Have you received the Decree of Praise?4 In short, my thoughts are in chaos; take it away with your letters. Oh! I wish the days would fly so that I could have news of you.

4. Here we continue to receive requests for houses and hospitals, and there are always new postulants and clothings. In a few days we have another.5 This year I am not calling the Superiors together, because I have not yet recovered from last year's expenses; I still have several debts; I shall call them another year if God grants me life.6

5. I assure you that for quite a while I have had a constant headache and am so swamped with business that I really don't know how to manage to do everything, always alone; and yet I try not to let a single packet go without writing to you.7

Greet Father Rocchi and the sisters; give them my love, tell them I await their letters, let them write to me; where are the promises?8 Goodbye, I am your

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The last letter received dated from 15 May 1879. Cf. L 291, n. 1

2 Cf. L 299,11.

3 ... this wretched human nature. The worry that besets her seems to her human weakness, almost a lack of trust in providence. But the pressing questions weigh on her mother's heart.

4 Cf. L 291,6 and 299,8.

5 On 18 July ten novices received the habit.

6 She used to call the house Superiors together in July or August for the spiritual exercises.

7 I let no mail boat go without writing to you.

She should give Sr. A. Illuminata what she asks for. She had written to her to send two strong, healthy Sisters: she sent two sick ones. She has acted selfishly!

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Give Sr. A. Illuminata whatever she needs, if they ask you for sheets, cups and other things; I am sure of your obedience.2 I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

2. P.S. How grieved I was to hear that you did not serve well at all! What, you sent to sit up at night one with an open blister and a cough? Oh! Dreadful wickedness! I tell you to choose two strong, healthy Sisters, and one has a blister and the other cannot walk!3 Thank you! That is enough for me to see that you are all only for yourselves; expect them back.4

She admits her to vows. She should be a peacemaker and know how to bear others' faults.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. In haste. You ask me for your vows2 and a line in my own hand; my God! It is little, but amid an abyss of things it is sometimes impossible for me.

2. Listen, go ahead and make your vows; and I urge you to get on well and try to keep the peace.

3. To bear3 others' faults is a holy thing. Jesus bears with us who offend him every minute; with that thought, everything goes well.

4. Goodbye, may the Lord bless you. For the other matters and the well, apply to the Deputies.4 I am your

Affectionate M. ROSA

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yes, make your vows;1 and if I do not write it is because I am unbelievably busy; but I can assure you I never let one of your letters pass without writing back, and always in my own hand, which I cannot do with everyone.
